methodological_rigor.justification: Combines network pharmacology (TCMSP, GeneCards, STRING, MCODE), AlphaFold-based molecular docking, TCGA bulk RNA analysis with CIBERSORT/ssGSEA, and in vitro (AGS, MGC803) plus in vivo (BALB/c nude xenograft) validation. Experimental details for in vitro dose-response curves and western blots are provided. Critical gaps: xenograft group size is not stated (only 'two cohorts' with alternate-day dosing), no randomization or blinding description in main text (author flags it as future work), statistics described only as 't-test or one-way ANOVA' with no multiplicity correction despite many pairwise comparisons, and no isotype IgG/positive controls in IHC/Western. Immunocompromised xenograft model precludes immunomodulatory claims, which the authors acknowledge.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Preclinical mechanistic study proposing quercetin/SERPINE1 axis as a gastric cancer therapeutic strategy. Quercetin is widely studied with known pharmacokinetic limitations (low bioavailability, authors acknowledge). No clinical translation is demonstrated and the TME claims are inferred from TCGA correlations. As preclinical cell/animal research, LoE maps to 5.

reporting_quality.justification: Animal work should follow ARRIVE; no ARRIVE checklist cited. Group sizes, randomization, blinding of outcome assessors, inclusion/exclusion criteria, adverse-event reporting, humane endpoints, and sample-size justification for the xenograft experiment are absent. Authors explicitly acknowledge this: 'plan also includes conducting corresponding randomization, blinding, and toxicity assessment experiments' (in future work). Cell line authentication beyond the institutional source is not reported. No data or code availability statement. Ethics approval is from an institutional Laboratory Animal Welfare Ethics Committee but no approval number is given.

novelty_literature.justification: Quercetin as an anti-gastric-cancer agent and SERPINE1 as a prognostic/metastatic gene in GC are both established topics. The specific combination and pathway analysis (AKT/MAPK, EMT via E/N-cadherin, Bax/Bcl-2) is incremental. Network pharmacology plus in vitro/in vivo validation of a natural product is a highly populated manuscript category. Molecular docking energies are cited comparatively but not benchmarked against a known SERPINE1 inhibitor in the same assay.

writing_presentation.justification: Generally clear and well-organized with standard network pharmacology structure. Language occasionally awkward ('Molecular docking demonstrated had a good binding affinity', 'TGF-beta-mediated immune suppression [25]'). Figures are appropriately referenced. Some percentages and claims are stated without source (e.g., 'SERPINE1 overexpression, observed in 78% of TCGA-STAD samples' - not directly substantiated in methods). Discussion cites plausible literature but occasionally overreaches ('superior to... baicalein', 'surpasses... tiplaxtinin') on the basis of single-study binding-energy comparisons.

key_strengths: Integration of network pharmacology, molecular docking, TCGA analysis, and in vitro plus in vivo experiments provides multi-layered evidence
Quercetin shows clear dose-dependent inhibition in two GC cell lines (AGS IC50 12.16 uM, MGC803 8.55 uM) with orthogonal assays (CCK-8, EdU, colony formation, Transwell, Annexin V/PI)
Identified SERPINE1 as a candidate core target via 137-gene intersection and MCODE hub analysis
Xenograft reported 78.4% tumor volume reduction at 50 mg/kg with stable body weights suggesting limited toxicity
Authors explicitly list limitations and future directions (patient-derived organoids, syngeneic models, nano-delivery)
key_concerns: Xenograft experiment lacks reported group size, randomization, blinding, and ARRIVE adherence, seriously limiting internal validity
Immune-infiltration/TME claims rely on TCGA correlations and an immunocompromised xenograft that cannot support the immunomodulatory conclusions drawn in the abstract and discussion
Molecular docking affinity comparisons to 'baicalein' and 'tiplaxtinin' are not from matched experiments and may overclaim quercetin's superiority
No multiplicity correction despite many pairwise comparisons; n/group and biological replicates not always stated
Authors themselves state that randomization, blinding, and toxicity assessment are future work - standard ARRIVE items that should have been in place
Data and code not shared; TCGA analysis pipeline parameters incomplete
chief_reviewer.rationale: Network pharmacology plus modest cell/animal validation study with standard design weaknesses and overstated immune-modulation claims; suitable at most for a Tier 4 specialty journal after major revisions addressing ARRIVE, proper controls, and more conservative interpretation.
